processing: Medium oxidation, strip-rolled and given a light to medium charcoal roast so that its fruit and plum-blossom aroma survive.
harvest_season: One spring picking, usually put between late April and mid-May, of shoots with two to four open leaves.
appearance_dry: Tight, slightly curved dark green to brown strips with a faint gloss and a sweet, fruity smell.
appearance_wet: Glossy, thick olive leaves with distinct red edges, which spread out plump and rounded.
taste_profile: Brighter than most rock tea: ripe plum and apricot, a plum-blossom floral note and a light roasted sweetness, with a clean mineral tail.

brewing.notes: Boiling water, porcelain gaiwan to show the fruit. Short early steeps; the aroma is at its best in the second and third infusions.

vintage_note: Spring harvest of the current year, roasted in early summer and sold from autumn with the year stated. Its light to medium roast means it is at its best within one to two years of harvest; it is rarely aged, and sets of the four famous bushes are usually the current year's tea.
description:
Shui Jin Gui, the golden water turtle, is one of the four famous bushes of Wuyi and the fruitiest of them: a rock tea with ripe plum, apricot and a floral note the Chinese sources compare to plum blossom, roasted lightly enough that none of it is lost.

The name comes with stories. The usual one has an abbot of Lei Shi temple finding the bush beside a ditch after heavy rain, its crossing branches looking from afar like a great golden turtle; another says the dense leaves shone like one. A further telling has a rainstorm carrying the bush downhill and a dispute over it going to court, which is hard to trace. The bush is still associated with the Niu Lan Keng area of the core scenic zone.

It is made like other yancha, picked mature and shaken into a medium oxidation, but makers generally stop the charcoal roast earlier than they would for Tie Luo Han or Shui Xian. That lighter hand keeps the liquor golden rather than amber and the taste on the fruit-and-flower side.

The second and third steeps are the best: aromatic, sweet, with a juicy acidity underneath. The body is lighter than a Rou Gui and the mineral finish shorter, which some drinkers hold against it and others find a relief. Boiling water and short steeps, and let the lid aroma tell you when to pour.

Shui Jin Gui is scarce and sells mostly as part of famous-bush sets or in small bags from specialist shops. Buy it by the current spring, from someone who names the year and the roast, and drink it within a couple of years; it is not a tea that gains from storage. If you like this side of Wuyi, Ban Tian Yao and Huang Guan Yin sit in the same fruity, lighter-roasted corner.
sources_note: The rainstorm and lawsuit story (usually dated to around 1919) is told as history in Wuyi but is presented here as a story.
history:
Shui Jin Gui is one of the four famous bushes of Wuyi, with Da Hong Pao, Bai Ji Guan and Tie Luo Han, and it is placed at Niu Lan Keng below She Ge Zhai peak.

The local legend has an abbot of Lei Shi temple finding the bush beside a ditch after heavy rain. Its crossing branches looked from afar like a great golden turtle, and a pool lay close by, hence the name. Another version credits dense leaves that shone like a golden turtle.

In more recent times it was a main export product of the Xiamen tea company, and after the state firms were reformed it became fairly easy to find on the market.
